title: Dattopant Thengadi National Board for Workers' Education and Development
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The Central Board for Workers' Education carries the founder's name.
body:
A worker who knows what the law says is harder to cheat and easier to organise. India has had a national body devoted to that idea for more than six decades. It began as the Central Board for Workers' Education and is now called the **Dattopant Thengadi National Board for Workers' Education and Development (DTNBWED)**. This post explains where it came from, what it does, what its recent numbers show and why it matters to unions.

## Background: a board born from a 1957 report

According to the Board's 2023-24 annual report, the **Central Board for Workers Education (CBWE)** was established on 16 September 1958 and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. It grew out of a 1957 expert report on workers' education, prepared with the Ford Foundation, which the Indian Labour Conference endorsed. The Board's own list of objectives refers to implementing the recommendations of that 1957 report, endorsed at the 15th Indian Labour Conference. It also refers to the Code of Discipline adopted at the 16th Indian Labour Conference in 1958, which shows how closely the Board's early work was linked to industrial relations.

The Board is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. The ILO's New Delhi office, in a 2023 address at a workshop held with the Board, noted that it has spent more than six decades preparing workers for changes in the world of work and that its wide network of facilities and trainers allows it to reach many workers and organisations.

## A new name

The annual report records that the Board was renamed the Dattopant Thengadi National Board for Workers Education and Development in **2016**. The name honours Dattopant Thengadi, who was born in 1920, founded the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh in 1955 and died in 2004. Thengadi was a trade union organiser and a thinker on labour and economic questions, and he served two terms in the Rajya Sabha between 1964 and 1976. A board devoted to workers' education carries his name because education, for him as for BMS, was a part of organising and not an afterthought.

## How it is organised

The Board's headquarters are in New Delhi, at Pusa Road. Its network runs through **50 Regional Directorates and 6 Sub-Regional Directorates**, grouped into zonal offices. The apex training institute, the Indian Institute of Workers Education, was set up in Mumbai in 1970.

The governance is **tripartite**, with members drawn from central and State Governments, central workers' and employers' organisations and educationists. The Union Minister for Labour and Employment is its President. Regional Advisory Committees, also tripartite, guide the regional work. This structure means that the programmes are, in principle, shaped by the three parties they concern.

## What it does

The Board's stated objectives are to build workers' awareness and education so they can take part effectively in the socio-economic development of society, industry and the nation. In practice it:

- trains workers of the **organised, unorganised and rural** sectors at national, regional, unit and village levels, with a focus on women, Scheduled Castes and Tribes, construction workers and other vulnerable groups;
- runs **Modular Training Programmes**, **Short Term Training Programmes** and sponsored programmes, as well as **Shramik Chaupal** sessions, which are community-level awareness gatherings;
- conducts **Training of Trainers** courses, which prepare volunteers and facilitators to carry the message into their own workplaces and villages;
- builds the **capacity of trade union office-bearers**, including training in trade unionism and in rights, duties and responsibilities;
- publicises welfare schemes for rural and unorganised workers and supports registration drives;
- gives **grants-in-aid** to registered trade unions and other institutions to run their own workers' education programmes;
- prepares curriculum and resource material in regional languages.

Its published objectives also include creating digital platforms and mobile applications for the employability and livelihoods of unorganised and migrant workers, and promoting financial inclusion through partnerships.

## Numbers from the latest report

The 2023-24 annual report gives a sense of the scale. The Board held about 11,300 programmes with roughly 779,000 participants in the year. Of these, 1,670 programmes reached 38,548 participants from the organised sector, while 9,591 programmes reached 739,695 participants from the unorganised sector, mostly through one-day short programmes. The Indian Institute of Workers Education ran 46 programmes with 1,176 participants. The report records grants-in-aid of Rs 105.13 crore received and Rs 105.30 crore utilised. Note that the report's own tables give slightly different totals for participants, so these should be read as approximate.

The numbers also tell a story about emphasis. Most of the Board's reach is among unorganised workers, who are the largest group in the labour force and the one with least access to information about their rights. It also shows that the organised sector gets fewer but, presumably, longer programmes.

## Why it matters to unions

Workers' education is a long-term investment. A union that explains the law to its members, and a worker who knows what the Code on Wages or the Social Security Code says about due dates, bonus and benefits, are both stronger in any negotiation. With the four Labour Codes being brought into force, the need for plain-language explanation is greater than it has been for a long time. The Board's role in awareness-cum-registration camps is relevant here, because registration on government portals is often the first step in claiming a benefit.

For BMS, which describes itself as a movement of *sanskar*, meaning values and character, as well as a trade union, education is at the heart of its work. The Board offers a government-supported channel, including grants-in-aid to registered unions, that unions of any affiliation can use.

## What remains to be done

Two things stand out. First, reach: 779,000 participants a year is large, but India's workforce is hundreds of millions, so the Board can only be a starting point and must work with unions and other bodies. Second, relevance: the Board is seeking Awarding Body status from the National Council for Vocational Education and Training, which would let it award recognised certificates and tie education to skills. Whether programmes keep pace with digital work, platform work and the new Codes will determine how useful they are.

## Learn more

The Board's website lists its Regional Directorates, courses and publications. A union office-bearer can start by finding the nearest Regional Directorate and asking about the next programme for trade union leaders or for unorganised workers in the area.
